reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Characterised by accumulation of surfactant-derived lipoproteinaceous material within the alveoli.

Three forms exist: autoimmune (over ninety per cent, mediated by anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies), secondary (haematological malignancy, inhaled dusts such as silica, immunodeficiency or infection) and hereditary (GM-CSF receptor or surfactant gene mutations, chiefly in children).
Insidious breathlessness and cough occur, and clinical signs are often disproportionately mild relative to imaging, a clinico-radiological dissociation.
HRCT shows 'crazy paving': ground-glass opacity with superimposed interlobular septal thickening in a geographical distribution.
Bronchoalveolar lavage is both diagnostic and therapeutic, yielding opaque, milky, periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive effluent.
An elevated serum anti-GM-CSF autoantibody confirms the autoimmune form.
Whole-lung lavage is the standard treatment for significant disease, with inhaled or subcutaneous GM-CSF an option in autoimmune disease.
There is an increased risk of secondary infection, including with Nocardia and mycobacteria.
reference.pathophysiology: Surfactant homeostasis depends on granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) signalling for alveolar macrophage maturation and surfactant clearance. In autoimmune disease, neutralising anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies impair macrophage function; secondary and hereditary forms disrupt the same pathway through reduced macrophage numbers or function or through receptor defects. The result is progressive alveolar filling with surfactant material that impairs gas exchange.
additionalDifferentials: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and other ground-glass interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Bronchoalveolar lavage with characteristic milky PAS-positive fluid
Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor, showing restriction and markedly reduced gas transfer
Serum lactate dehydrogenase, which is often raised
Transbronchial or surgical biopsy if lavage is non-diagnostic
Screening for secondary causes with blood film or marrow examination, occupational dust history and immune function tests
redFlags: Superimposed opportunistic infection with Nocardia, mycobacteria or fungi
Rapid deterioration suggesting secondary disease from a haematological malignancy
reference.prognosis: Autoimmune disease often responds well to whole-lung lavage with good long-term survival; the prognosis of secondary disease depends on the underlying disorder, and some cases resolve spontaneously.
pitfalls: Mistaking crazy paving for infection or pulmonary oedema
Not measuring the anti-GM-CSF autoantibody to classify disease
Missing an underlying haematological malignancy in secondary disease
Failing to consider opportunistic infection when a patient deteriorates
